# Berner_Immanuel_1898

> 📷 **Photos in this folder**: 5 files — 1 full-stone shot + 4 lichen close-ups
> 🗓️ **Captured**: 29 April 2026, ~11:00
> 📍 **Site**: Templerfriedhof Jerusalem (Templer Cemetery), Emek Refaim 37, German Colony

---

## 🪦 Gravestone Identification

### Original Inscription (German)
```
IMMANUEL BERNER
GEB. 2. NOV. 1849
IN ROTHENBERG BEI STUTTGART
GEST. 27. NOV. 1898
DEIN REICH KOMME.
MATTH. 6.10.
```
*Inscription partially obscured by weathering in field photograph (IMG_3969); exact dates confirmed via Tempelgesellschaft registry.*

### English Translation
```
IMMANUEL BERNER
BORN 2 NOVEMBER 1849
IN ROTHENBERG NEAR STUTTGART
DIED 27 NOVEMBER 1898
THY KINGDOM COME.
MATTHEW 6:10.
```
*(From the Lord's Prayer — a distinctly Tempelgesellschaft theological expression of the movement's millennial expectation)*

### Hebrew Translation / תרגום לעברית
```
עמנואל ברנר
נולד 2 בנובמבר 1849
ברוטנברג ליד שטוטגרט
נפטר 27 בנובמבר 1898
תָּבֹא מַלְכוּתֶךָ.
מתי ו', י'.
```
*(ציטוט מתפילת "אבינו שבשמים" — "תָּבֹא מַלְכוּתֶךָ" — מרכזי באידיאולוגיה של תנועת טמפלר, שראתה בעלייה לארץ הקודש הגשמה של ממלכת ה')*

### Identification

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Surname(s)** | Berner |
| **Given name(s)** | Immanuel |
| **Born** | 02.11.1849 |
| **Died** | 27.11.1898 |
| **Age at death** | 49 |
| **Stone age (as of 2026)** | 128 years (since 1898) |
| **Place of birth** | Rothenberg bei Stuttgart, Germany |
| **Place of death** | Jerusalem (presumed) |
| **Inscription material** | German |

### Biographical context
Immanuel Berner (1849–1898) was born in Rothenberg bei Stuttgart (Württemberg, Germany) — the heartland of the Tempelgesellschaft movement, which was founded in 1861 in Württemberg by Christoph Hoffmann Sr. Berner died in Jerusalem on 27 November 1898, exactly 25 days after his 49th birthday. He would have emigrated to Jerusalem as a young adult, consistent with the wave of Württemberg Templer families who settled in the German Colony (Emek Refaim) following its 1873 founding. His gravestone — a substantial limestone obelisk/column monument on a multi-step pedestal base — suggests a family of some standing within the community. The epitaph "Thy Kingdom Come" (Matt. 6:10, from the Lord's Prayer) is theologically central to the Tempelgesellschaft's mission: they believed that emigrating to the Holy Land was the literal fulfillment of building God's Kingdom on earth. Confirmed in the Tempelgesellschaft registry (entry id=83, position 06-I).

**Sources consulted**:
- Tempelgesellschaft gravestone registry (entry id=83): https://www.tempelgesellschaft.de/de/geschichte/historische-friedhoefe/verzeichnis-grabstaetten.php?id=83&detail=1 (accessed 29 April 2026)
- Tempelgesellschaft historical overview: https://www.tempelgesellschaft.de (accessed 29 April 2026)

**Confidence**: `medium`
- The Tempelgesellschaft registry directly matches name, birth date, birthplace, death date, and epitaph. The Württemberg Templer connection is well-documented. No personal biographical detail beyond what the stone and registry record.

> [!todo] Verify against authoritative source
> Cross-reference with **Eisler, J. & Gräf, U. (2023). _Der historische Friedhof der Tempelgesellschaft in Jerusalem_** (Vol. 1, ISBN 978-3-944051-23-9). The book documents ~1,000 names and ~400 full biographies with photographs of the gravestones.

---

## 🦠 Lichen Analysis

### Photos analyzed
- IMG_3970.jpeg — obelisk base torus/moulding; Caloplaca rosettes on curved surface
- IMG_3971.jpeg — top edge/ledge of stone plinth; multi-species zonation across edge
- IMG_3972.jpeg — individual Caloplaca rosettes close-up showing aged-centre morphology
- IMG_3973.jpeg — column/obelisk moulding ribs; multiple Caloplaca rosettes on dark grey stone

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: Jerusalem limestone (grey-white, coarse-grained) — standard for large Templer monuments at this cemetery; large obelisk/column form on stepped pedestal base
- **Surface condition**: Moderately weathered; column shaft relatively clean; base mouldings and ledges show heaviest accumulation
- **Aspect (if inferable from photo)**: Mixed aspects — column has all-round exposure; curved mouldings at base provide sheltered micro-environments

### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1
- **Color**: Bright yellow-orange to orange
- **Thallus type**: Placodioid (lobate margin, pale/weathered centre in older thalli)
- **Growth pattern**: Discrete rosettes, ~1.5–3 cm diameter; each rosette clearly delineated from neighbours; abundant on curved/convex moulding surfaces (IMG_3970, IMG_3973)
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Not clearly resolved in these shots; apothecia probable but not confirmed
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone moulding; slight etching at lobe tips suspected
- **Approx. coverage**: Dominant on moulded surfaces (~40–60% of IMG_3970 and IMG_3973 fields)
- **Likely genus**: **_Caloplaca_** (likely _C. aurantia_)
- **Confidence in ID**: `high`
- **Reasoning**: Bright yellow-orange discrete placodioid rosettes with clearly lobate margins on calcareous moulded surfaces — classic _Caloplaca aurantia_ morphology, consistent with all other cluster observations at this cemetery. Pale weathered centre surrounded by actively growing orange margin is characteristic of mature _C. aurantia_ thalli.

#### Lichen #2
- **Color**: Black
- **Thallus type**: Endolithic / very thin crustose
- **Growth pattern**: Irregular patches and background staining on vertical stone faces; forms distinct band on top edge (IMG_3971)
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Pin-point perithecia probable
- **Substrate interaction**: At or below stone surface
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate (~20–30% on vertical faces; visible as dark band in IMG_3971)
- **Likely genus**: **_Verrucaria nigrescens_**
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Black endolithic crust forming a distinct band/zone adjacent to orange _Caloplaca_ on limestone — characteristic _Verrucaria nigrescens_ pattern. The sharp boundary between orange and black zones in IMG_3971 is diagnostic of inter-specific competition at the thallus margin.

#### Lichen #3
- **Color**: Grey-white to pale grey
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, flush
- **Growth pattern**: Scattered patches and diffuse background on vertical faces; present in zones between orange and black species
- **Reproductive structures visible**: None clearly visible
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate (~15–20% of vertical faces)
- **Likely genus**: **_Aspicilia_** sp. or **_Lecanora muralis_**
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Grey-white flush crustose patches in intermediate zones between _Caloplaca_ and _Verrucaria_ — consistent with _Aspicilia calcarea_ or _Lecanora muralis_, both common at this cemetery and at this relative position in the inter-species competition mosaic.

### Ecology & interpretation
- The column obelisk form of GS05 provides multiple aspect exposures (N/S/E/W) on the same stone — making it a potentially valuable multi-aspect lichen comparison study in a single monument.
- _Caloplaca_ rosettes strongly prefer convex curved moulding surfaces (IMG_3970, IMG_3973); this preference for convex geometry may relate to reduced water-film duration after rain on convex surfaces, favouring faster-drying surface lichen.
- The sharp orange/_Verrucaria_ boundary (IMG_3971) on the ledge top edge is a textbook inter-species competition boundary visible at a single photo — research illustration priority.
- Stone age: 126 years at time of photography (d. 1898); moderate-to-heavy coverage (~40–60% on curved surfaces) is consistent with expected succession.
- Pollution signal: crustose-only community (no foliose species) consistent with moderate urban pollution. _Caloplaca_ dominance aligns with expected eutrophication tolerance (bird excretion along the top mouldings).
- Birthplace (Rothenberg bei Stuttgart) situates Berner squarely in the Württemberg Tempelgesellschaft heartland — epitaph "Thy Kingdom Come" reflects the movement's founding theological premise.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). Where the photo is ambiguous, this is noted explicitly.

## 🦠 Lichen Analysis

### Photos analyzed
- IMG_4044.jpeg (full-stone shot)
- IMG_4045.jpeg (close-up)
- IMG_4046.jpeg (close-up)
- IMG_4047.jpeg (close-up)

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: Dark grey limestone — stone appears significantly darker than the cream Jerusalem limestone typical of Templer graves; either a dark imported limestone, basalt-region stone, or very deeply stained pale stone
- **Surface condition**: Heavily weathered; surface almost entirely colonised; carved lettering remains legible
- **Aspect (if inferable from photo)**: Unclear; high endolithic coverage suggests possible north or east-facing aspect with high moisture retention

### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1
- **Color**: Dark grey to near-black
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, endolithic (growing within stone mineral matrix rather than on surface)
- **Growth pattern**: Continuous dense mat; stone surface appears uniformly dark; barely distinguishable from stone at macro scale; tiny black perithecioid fruiting bodies just visible under close inspection in IMG_4045 and IMG_4046
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Perithecia (immersed, black, dot-like) — characteristic flask-shaped fruiting bodies of pyrenolichens
- **Substrate interaction**: Deeply endolithic — organism penetrates into stone mineral matrix; surface expression minimal
- **Approx. coverage**: Dominant — estimated 85–95% of stone surface; the stone's dark appearance is largely the lichen organism
- **Likely genus**: **_Verrucaria nigrescens_**
- **Confidence in ID**: `high`
- **Reasoning**: Near-black endolithic crustose with immersed black perithecia on calcareous stone in a Mediterranean context is the classic description of _Verrucaria nigrescens_ (Verrucariales); this species is the most common blackening agent on limestone in the Jerusalem area and Mediterranean basin generally

#### Lichen #2
- **Color**: Orange-yellow to yellow-green, granular
- **Thallus type**: Crustose
- **Growth pattern**: Scattered patches amid dark _Verrucaria_ mat; clearly visible in IMG_4047 as a bright orange-yellow island
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Small apothecia visible in brightest patch
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush to stone surface
- **Approx. coverage**: Minor — ~5–10% of total surface
- **Likely genus**: **_Caloplaca_** sp. or **_Candelariella_** sp.
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Orange-yellow patch amid dark endolithic community is consistent with either _Caloplaca_ (orange morph, K+ purple) or _Candelariella_ (yellow-green, K–); chemical spot test needed to distinguish

### Ecology & interpretation
- **Exposure and moisture**: The dominance of _Verrucaria nigrescens_ — a shade-tolerant and moisture-retaining endolithic species — suggests this stone receives lower direct insolation than neighbouring stones; possibly in shade of wall or tree
- **Stone age signal**: Dense _Verrucaria_ domination and deep endolithic penetration is consistent with an older stone (pre-1965 placement suggests possible ≥60 years colonisation)
- **Biodeterioration concern**: Endolithic lichens such as _Verrucaria_ are among the most destructive to stone fabric — the organism dissolves carbonate mineral directly. The very high coverage observed here represents significant ongoing material loss at the stone surface
- **Pollution tolerance**: _Verrucaria nigrescens_ is a pollution-tolerant nitrophyte; its dominance is consistent with roadside or urban-margin placement

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). Where the photo is ambiguous, this is noted explicitly.

> 📷 **Photos in this folder**: 5 files — 1 full-stone shot + 4 lichen close-ups
> 🗓️ **Captured**: 29 April 2026, ~10:45
> 📍 **Site**: Templerfriedhof Jerusalem (Templer Cemetery), Emek Refaim 37, German Colony

---

## 🪦 Gravestone Identification

### Original Inscription (German)
```
DAVID EPPINGER
GEB. DEN 5. JAN. 1801
GEST. DEN 16. JUNI 1879
SELIG SIND DIE TOTEN
DIE IN DEM HERRN STERBEN
VON NUN AN

```

### English Translation
```
DAVID EPPINGER
BORN 5 JANUARY 1801

BLESSED ARE THE DEAD
WHO DIE IN THE LORD
FROM THIS TIME FORWARD
REV. 14:13
```

### Hebrew Translation / תרגום לעברית
```
דוד אפינגר
נולד 5 בינואר 1801
נפטר 16 ביוני 1879
אַשְׁרֵי הַמֵּתִים
הַמֵּתִים בַּאדוֹן מֵעַתָּה

```
*(פסוק זהה מחרות גם על חלקה שכנה — מצבת קתרינה שמידט, גרבסטון 03)*

### Identification

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Surname(s)** | Eppinger |
| **Given name(s)** | David |
| **Born** | 05.01.1801 |
| **Died** | 16.06.1879 |
| **Age at death** | 78 |
| **Stone age (as of 2026)** | 147 years (since 1879) |
| **Place of birth** | Not shown on stone |
| **Place of death** | Jerusalem (presumed) |
| **Inscription material** | German |

### Biographical context
David Eppinger (1801–1879) is one of the oldest individuals documented in this study — born in 1801 and dying at 78 years of age on 16 June 1879. The Tempelgesellschaft Jerusalem colony was established in 1873, meaning David arrived (or settled) in Jerusalem at approximately age 72, positioning him as a member of the founding generation of the colony. He died just six years after the colony's establishment. Notably, his gravestone is **not registered** in the Tempelgesellschaft's online historical cemetery database (which lists only "Gotthilf Immanuel Eppinger," b. 1880, and "Martha Eppinger," b. 1891 — both children, likely later-generation family members). David Eppinger's absence from the database may reflect gaps in the 2004 survey coverage of earliest-generation graves, or administrative omission. The Eppinger surname appears elsewhere in the Tempelgesellschaft record as an established Templer family in Jerusalem. Insufficient web evidence to expand biography further.

**Sources consulted**:
- Tempelgesellschaft gravestone registry (alpha=E): https://www.tempelgesellschaft.de/de/geschichte/historische-friedhoefe/verzeichnis-grabstaetten.php?group=All&alpha=E (accessed 29 April 2026) — David Eppinger NOT listed; only later Eppinger children found
- Visual analysis of IMG_3964 (full stone)

**Confidence**: `low`
- Stone inscription is clearly legible and confirms name and dates. However, the individual is absent from the Tempelgesellschaft registry, and no secondary biographical sources were located.

> [!todo] Verify against authoritative source
> Cross-reference with **Eisler, J. & Gräf, U. (2023). _Der historische Friedhof der Tempelgesellschaft in Jerusalem_** (Vol. 1, ISBN 978-3-944051-23-9). As a founding-generation settler (d. 1879), David Eppinger may be documented with more detail in this definitive reference.

---

## 🦠 Lichen Analysis

### Photos analyzed
- IMG_3965.jpeg — yellow-green crustose thallus with orange-brown apothecia
- IMG_3966.jpeg — amber-brown glistening crust (possibly water-wetted lichen)
- IMG_3967.jpeg — classic tri-zone: bright orange placodioid / black crust / grey-white crust
- IMG_3968.jpeg — stone plinth/base at ground level; orange-yellow Caloplaca on horizontal moulding

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: Jerusalem limestone (calcareous) — rectangular plaque on pedestal base; typical cream-grey limestone
- **Surface condition**: Moderately weathered plaque face; stone base shows heavier lichen accumulation, particularly on horizontal ledges
- **Aspect (if inferable from photo)**: Vertical plaque face, upright orientation; base at ground level shows enhanced moisture retention

### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1
- **Color**: Yellow-green to olive-yellow
- **Thallus type**: Crustose; thin; continuous
- **Growth pattern**: Continuous mat with discrete small apothecia (IMG_3965)
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Apothecia present — orange-brown disc, ~0.3–0.8 mm diameter
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate (~20–30% of plaque field in IMG_3965)
- **Likely genus**: **_Candelariella_** sp. or **_Caloplaca variabilis_**
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Yellow-green crustose thallus with orange-brown apothecia on limestone — consistent with _Candelariella_ spp. (e.g., _C. vitellina_) or the yellow crustose form of _Caloplaca variabilis_. The relatively dull yellow-green colour (not bright orange) makes _Candelariella_ more likely.

#### Lichen #2
- **Color**: Amber-brown to orange-brown; glistening/glossy surface
- **Thallus type**: Crustose; appears unusually glistening
- **Growth pattern**: Large irregular patches (IMG_3966); surface has wet/gelatinous appearance
- **Reproductive structures visible**: None clearly resolvable in glistening surface
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone; possible moisture retention
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate (~30–40% of IMG_3966 field)
- **Likely genus**: **_Caloplaca_** sp. (water-wetted) or unknown brown crustose
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: The glistening surface texture is atypical and may reflect water-wetted thallus (recent rain or heavy dew), which can make _Caloplaca_ appear much more amber/brown than its dry orange-red colour. Cannot rule out a distinct brown crustose species without dry-state comparison.

#### Lichen #3
- **Color**: Bright yellow-orange (placodioid rosettes) / black (crustose) / grey-white (crustose)
- **Thallus type**: Mixed — placodioid (lobate) for orange; endolithic/crustose for black; crustose flush for grey-white
- **Growth pattern**: Classic tri-zone zonation (IMG_3967) — bright orange lobed thallus transitioning to black zone, with grey-white patches in between
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Orange apothecia visible in placodioid zone; black perithecia in black zone
- **Substrate interaction**: Placodioid raised at lobes; black zone endolithic; grey-white flush
- **Approx. coverage**: Co-dominant (~60–70% total of IMG_3967 field across all three morphotypes)
- **Likely genera**:
  - Orange zone: **_Caloplaca aurantia_** — `high` confidence
  - Black zone: **_Verrucaria nigrescens_** — `medium` confidence
  - Grey-white zone: **_Aspicilia_** sp. or **_Lecanora muralis_** — `low` confidence
- **Reasoning**: The tri-zone pattern is a well-documented succession/competition pattern on Jerusalem limestone. _Caloplaca aurantia_ occupies the most exposed surface; _Verrucaria nigrescens_ establishes in zones of differential moisture or pH; _Aspicilia_ / _Lecanora muralis_ occupy intermediate conditions.

#### Lichen #4
- **Color**: Bright yellow-orange
- **Thallus type**: Placodioid (lobate)
- **Growth pattern**: Multiple discrete rosettes on horizontal/curved base moulding (IMG_3968); each rosette ~1.5–2.5 cm diameter
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Not resolved at this scale
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with curved stone surface
- **Approx. coverage**: Dominant on horizontal moulding (~40–50% of IMG_3968 field)
- **Likely genus**: **_Caloplaca_** (likely _C. aurantia_)
- **Confidence in ID**: `high`
- **Reasoning**: Bright yellow-orange placodioid rosettes on horizontal limestone base moulding — identical to the pattern observed in GS01, GS03, and GS05 clusters. Consistent with _Caloplaca aurantia_ preference for convex/horizontal exposed calcareous surfaces.

### Ecology & interpretation
- Stone dated 1879 — oldest dated stone in this 6-cluster study (145 years at time of photography). Moderate coverage (~30–40%) suggests good accumulation over this timespan.
- The tri-zone pattern (IMG_3967) is the clearest textbook example of multi-species lichen zonation in the entire 6-cluster set — strong research illustration potential.
- Pollution signal: mix of _Caloplaca_, _Verrucaria_, and _Aspicilia_ (no foliose species) is consistent with moderate urban pollution, as expected for the German Colony residential area.
- Ground-level horizontal mouldings (IMG_3968) show densest _Caloplaca_ coverage — water runoff from rain concentrates at the base, providing enhanced moisture and dissolved mineral nutrients.
- **Notable**: David Eppinger (b. 1801) is absent from the Tempelgesellschaft registry, making this stone historically significant as a potentially unregistered founding-generation grave.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). The amber-brown glistening crust (Lichen #2, IMG_3966) is specifically flagged as anomalous and requires dry-state comparison photography.

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: Jerusalem limestone (calcareous) — white/cream, medium-grained; typical local nari limestone
- **Surface condition**: Generally well-preserved; letter grooves show painted fill (blue/dark) with overlying biological staining; base of stone significantly colonized by moss; vertical face above base shows lichen.
- **Aspect (if inferable)**: The presence of a dense basal moss mat suggests this stone face receives limited direct sunlight, consistent with a north-facing or shaded orientation, or proximity to a wall/adjacent stone that retains moisture.

### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1 — Cyanobacterial biofilm / staining in paint-filled letter grooves
- **Color**: Blue-grey to dark blue-green; overlying the paint fill in grooves
- **Thallus type**: Biofilm / proto-crustose (cyanobacterial film rather than true lichen thallus)
- **Growth pattern**: Coating groove interiors and spreading slightly onto surrounding stone
- **Reproductive structures visible**: None (vegetative film)
- **Substrate interaction**: Colonizing painted groove surface and adjacent limestone; cyanobacteria can penetrate stone surface (endolithic)
- **Approx. coverage**: Dominant inside grooves; trace on flat face
- **Likely genus**: Cyanobacteria (likely **_Gloeocapsa_** sp. or **_Chroococcus_** sp.); possibly early successional biofilm including non-lichenised algae
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Blue-grey/dark biofilm staining on painted limestone grooves in a Mediterranean cemetery context is consistent with cyanobacterial (blue-green algae) colonization, which is the typical pioneer in the crustose lichen succession sequence. The blue/dark color seen on the paint fill (IMG_4078) may be a combination of the original paint color and overlying biological darkening. Photo resolution insufficient for confident genera assignment.

#### Lichen #2 — Green bryophyte (moss) mat at stone base
- **Color**: Green (vivid, indicating active growth)
- **Thallus type**: Bryophyte — NOT a lichen (no fungal partner); included here as a key component of the substrate colonization community
- **Growth pattern**: Dense mat at base of stone, extending from ground level upward ~5–10 cm onto vertical face
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Possible sporophytes not clearly resolved; leaf structure confirms bryophyte
- **Substrate interaction**: Growing at stone-soil interface; likely anchored in soil and colonizing stone face upward; retaining moisture against stone
- **Approx. coverage**: Dominant at stone base (~80–90% of base zone)
- **Likely genus**: Likely **_Bryum_** sp. or **_Tortula_** sp. — most common calcareous-substrate mosses in Mediterranean urban environments
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Dense green mat with visible "leaf" structure in IMG_4081/4082 confirms bryophyte; genus-level ID requires microscopy. *Bryum* and *Tortula* are the two most frequently recorded calcareous-substrate mosses in Jerusalem cemeteries.

#### Lichen #3 — Yellow-orange Caloplaca rosettes on vertical stone face above moss
- **Color**: Yellow-orange to amber
- **Thallus type**: Placodioid — lobate rosette
- **Growth pattern**: Discrete rosettes, 1–4 cm diameter, on vertical face above the basal moss belt
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Apothecia visible — darker orange discs, lecanorine type
- **Substrate interaction**: Adnate to stone surface; spreading on limestone face
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate on vertical face above moss belt (~15–25%)
- **Likely genus**: ***Caloplaca*** sp. (possibly *C. aurantia* or *C. saxicola*)
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Yellow-orange placodioid rosettes on vertical calcareous limestone face is the textbook presentation of *Caloplaca aurantia*, the most common orange lichen on Jerusalem limestone. The position above the basal moss belt is typical — *Caloplaca* colonizes the drier, better-lit zone above the permanently moist base.

#### Lichen #4 — White crustose patches (background, stone face)
- **Color**: White to pale cream
- **Thallus type**: Crustose
- **Growth pattern**: Irregular patches on stone face, background to Caloplaca rosettes
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Not resolved
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone
- **Approx. coverage**: Low to moderate (~10–20%)
- **Likely genus**: ***Aspicilia*** sp. or ***Lecanora*** sp.
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Typical background crustose on Jerusalem limestone; morphology not sufficiently resolved for genus distinction.

### Ecology & interpretation
- **Basal moisture gradient**: The distribution of biological communities on this stone clearly shows a moisture gradient: dense moss at base (highest moisture, least light), *Caloplaca* rosettes on the drier vertical face above (more light, less moisture), and cyanobacterial biofilm in sheltered letter grooves. This gradient is a micro-scale version of the moisture gap described in the project framework.
- **Shading and north-facing inference**: The dense moss mat (requiring sustained moisture and shade) strongly suggests this stone is north-facing or significantly shaded by adjacent vegetation or structures. A south-facing Jerusalem limestone stone of similar age would typically show *Caloplaca*-dominant coverage even at the base, with much less bryophyte development.
- **Inscription legibility**: The cyanobacterial staining in the letter grooves (IMG_4078) is beginning to obscure the blue-painted inscriptions. Without intervention, biological crust succession will progress to crustose lichen within the grooves over 10–20 years, potentially making the inscription illegible — the same process documented in GS22. Martha Eppinger's stone thus documents an earlier stage of the "memory erasure" process.
- **Pollution tolerance**: The presence of *Caloplaca* (moderate pollution-tolerant) and bryophytes (often pollution-tolerant in Mediterranean climates) is consistent with the moderate urban baseline of the German Colony.
- **Caliper measurement** (IMG_4083 ~67 mm): This appears to measure lichen or moss thickness, or stone edge width at a specific point — useful quantitative data for the project's mapping work.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). The cyanobacterial biofilm (Lichen #1) and the bryophyte (Lichen #2) in particular require physical examination for any reliable genus-level identification. ### Biographical context

Jacob Imberger (1849–1912) was a member of the Jerusalem German Templer community, dying at age 62 — just one day before what would have been his 63rd birthday, a poignant coincidence preserved by the stone's dates. ### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1 — dark crustose background
- **Color**: Dark grey-green to grey-black
- **Thallus type**: Crustose (granular to areolate)
- **Growth pattern**: Continuous background mat; granular texture with moderate areolation (IMG_4014)
- **Reproductive structures visible**: None clearly visible

- **Approx. coverage**: Dominant on older stone faces — ~50–60% of total surface

#### Lichen #2 — white-grey placodioid rosette (**key identification**)
- **Color**: White to pale grey; centre more areolate/cracked, lobes cleaner at margin
- **Thallus type**: Placodioid (clearly lobate with well-defined radial marginal lobes)

- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone surface; marginal lobes slightly raised from substrate
- **Approx. coverage**: Multiple rosettes present; individually ~5–10 cm diameter; together ~15–20% of observed stone face
- **Likely genus**: **_Lecanora muralis_**
- **Confidence in ID**: `high`
- **Reasoning**: Well-defined circular white-grey placodioid rosette with raised radial marginal lobes, pale lecanorine apothecia concentrated centrally, on a calcareous upright urban limestone surface — this is textbook _Lecanora muralis_ morphology per the project cheatsheet. #### Lichen #3 — yellow-green small apothecia
- **Color**: Bright yellow-green to sulphur-yellow
- **Thallus type**: Crustose (thin; thallus largely inconspicuous; apothecia prominent)
- **Growth pattern**: Small scattered apothecia on dark crustose background (IMG_4017)
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Apothecia — small (0.3–0.7 mm), yellow-green, biatorine-type, slightly convex
- **Substrate interaction**: Epilithic; seated within or on surface of dark background crust
- **Approx. coverage**: Trace to low — scattered, ~5% of IMG_4017 frame
- **Likely genus**: **_Candelariella_** (likely _C. vitellina_ or _C. aurella_)
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Bright yellow-green small biatorine apothecia on a calcareous substrate with an inconspicuous thallus is characteristic of _Candelariella vitellina_ or _C. aurella_, both documented in the expected Jerusalem limestone community (project cheatsheet). Small _Caloplaca_ with yellow-green pigmentation is also possible; UV fluorescence test (positive for _Caloplaca_ rhizocarpic acid-bearing taxa) would differentiate.

#### Lichen #4 — grey-white patch crustose (inscription zone)
- **Color**: Grey-white to pale cream
- **Thallus type**: Crustose (smooth to slightly areolate)
- **Growth pattern**: Patches following carved letter surfaces and adjacent flat stone zones (visible in multiple close-ups)
- **Reproductive structures visible**: None clearly visible
- **Substrate interaction**: Colonises carved letter grooves and adjacent flat surfaces; follows micro-relief of inscription
- **Approx. coverage**: Low to moderate — ~10–15% in inscription-area close-ups
- **Likely genus**: **_Aspicilia_** sp. or pale crustose (indeterminate)
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Grey-white crustose without visible reproductive structures in inscription zone; genus-level assignment not possible from colour alone. Lichen colonisation of carved letter surfaces is a key research observation for this project (biological reading of inscription relief).

### Ecology & interpretation
- Gravestone_15 hosts the **richest and best-documented lichen community in this batch (G12–G16)**, with 12 dedicated close-up images revealing at least 4 morphologically distinct taxa.
- The confirmed presence of _Lecanora muralis_ (high-confidence placodioid rosettes, IMG_4015 and IMG_4016) is significant: this species is a well-known urban and sub-urban calcareous indicator that tolerates moderate air pollution and is characteristic of sun-exposed limestone walls and monuments throughout the Mediterranean. Its dominance here is consistent with the south-facing, well-lit exposure of an upright urban stele.
- _Candelariella vitellina_-type (IMG_4017) adds a further pollution-tolerant indicator; this species is common in moderately enriched (nitrophytic) environments, which may reflect bird perching or atmospheric nitrogen deposition on the upper stone surfaces.
- The dark crustose background (Verrucaria-type) underlying the _Lecanora_ rosettes represents an earlier or co-occurring colonist in the community succession.
- Lichen colonisation of carved inscription surfaces (letter grooves) is directly relevant to the project's research question about biological agencies modifying stone memory — lichens are here actively re-inscribing and obscuring the human inscription.
- Stone age at survey: ~114 years (death 1912). The diverse, mature community is consistent with this age on a calcareous upright surface.
- No foliose or fruticose species observed — consistent with urban pollution exposure and calcareous substrate selectivity.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). _Lecanora muralis_ identification (Lichen #2) is rated `high` confidence as the morphology is textbook-clear in two independent images. ### Additional lichen observations from IMG_4064 (the merged-in cluster-21 close-up)
The macro into the "RA…" letters of "KRAFFT" shows a **completely different colonization regime** from the orange Caloplaca dominant elsewhere on this stone:
- Sparse, granular, **yellow-green to khaki dotting** distributed across the smooth pink stone surface — most consistent with **incipient *Candelariella vitellina*** (small egg-yolk-yellow granular crustose) and/or very early *Verrucaria* (small dark perithecia) on a relatively clean inscription panel

- The contrast between the dense Caloplaca aurantia rosettes elsewhere on this stone and the sparse early-stage community right next to the inscription is itself a research-relevant in-situ observation about **how the inscribed surface resists colonization** (smoother face, possibly more recently cleaned, less moisture retention)

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: **Pink/rose-coloured stone** — confirmed in IMG_4050 where the substrate colour between lichen patches is distinctly pinkish-cream, NOT the pale buff/grey of standard Jerusalem limestone. Likely a regional sandstone, rose-coloured limestone variant (such as Ramleh stone), or quarried pink stone imported for the grave. - **Surface condition**: Moderately weathered; carved letterforms visible; surface shows some spalling at edges

- **Growth pattern**: Rosette — well-developed, multiple expanding colonies visible in IMG_4051
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Orange apothecia present; disc slightly raised and darker than lobe margins
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush to stone; pink substrate visible at colony margins confirming stone colour
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate — ~25–35% of stone face
- **Likely genus**: **_Caloplaca aurantia_**
- **Confidence in ID**: `high`
- **Reasoning**: Bright orange-yellow placodioid rosette with orange apothecia on a calcareous substrate is characteristic of _Caloplaca aurantia_; the pink stone substrate does not affect the ID — this species colonises any calcium-rich surface

#### Lichen #2
- **Color**: Yellow-green to olive, granular
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, granular to finely areolate
- **Growth pattern**: Patches visible in IMG_4052; scattered between _Caloplaca_ colonies
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Not clearly distinguishable at this resolution
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush to stone
- **Approx. coverage**: Minor to moderate — ~10–15%
- **Likely genus**: **_Candelariella_** sp. (possibly _C. vitellina_ or _C. aurella_)
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Yellow-green granular crustose on calcium-rich stone is consistent with _Candelariella_ spp.; visual separation from yellow _Caloplaca_ morphs requires K spot test

#### Lichen #3
- **Color**: Black, dot-like
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, endolithic-suspected
- **Growth pattern**: Scattered black dots/perithecioid structures visible in close-ups
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Perithecia (immersed black dots)

> IMG_4050 shows a distinct **teal or turquoise blue-green colour specifically within the carved letter grooves** of the inscription, not present on the flat stone face between letters. Two hypotheses:
> 1. **Paint remnant**: The inscription may have originally been painted (common practice for carved Templer inscriptions); the teal pigment, possibly a copper-based paint, survives only in the protected groove environment where it is sheltered from UV and rain erosion.
> 2. **Biological colonisation**: A cyanobacterial or algal film (e.g., _Gloeocapsa_ sp., _Trentepohlia_ sp.) has established specifically within the letter grooves where moisture retention and shade create a microhabitat different from the exposed stone face.
> A field visit with a hand lens and possibly a UV torch would help distinguish residual paint from biological pigment. This observation should be flagged in the cemetery-wide analysis as a potential indicator of painted inscription practice among the Templer community.

### Ecology & interpretation
- **Substrate uniqueness**: The pink/rose stone is ecologically significant — different mineral chemistry (if sandstone vs limestone) could alter which lichen species colonise; the presence of _Caloplaca aurantia_ confirms there is sufficient calcium in the substrate to support calcicolous species
- **Coverage**: Moderate overall (~40–60%); stone placed c.1934 (~91 years) — moderate coverage rate consistent with partly shaded or partly sheltered location
- **Microhabitat in letter grooves**: Grooves act as protected refuges — sheltered from direct rain wash and UV; teal/turquoise organism (biological or paint) reflects the distinct microhabitat within the carved inscription

> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). ## 🦠 Lichen Analysis

### Photos analyzed
- **IMG_3974.jpeg, IMG_3975.jpeg** — two full-stone shots from slightly different angles. Front (inscribed) face appears very clean: only faint dark stippling, possibly incipient *Verrucaria* perithecia visible at very low coverage (<5 %).
- **IMG_3976.jpeg** — overview of the stone's **horizontal upper surface** (the cap/cornice on top of the inscribed front panel). This surface tells a completely different story from the front face: a dense, vivid **yellow-orange placodioid rosette community** carpets the top, mixed with grey-white substrate patches and occasional dark perithecial dots.
- **IMG_3977.jpeg, IMG_3978.jpeg** — macros into the same orange community, with surface visibly wet/sprayed (one of the project's documented field techniques — the spray reveals the apothecial structure of *Caloplaca*).
- **IMG_3979.jpeg** — adjacent close-up showing the boundary between the orange Caloplaca colony and the bare grey stone.

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: White/cream marble or light Jerusalem limestone (highly reflective; bright stone colour, smooth carved face)
- **Surface condition**: Inscribed front face is exceptionally well preserved (smooth, near-clean); horizontal top surface is heavily colonized — a stark **aspect contrast** within a single stone
- **Aspect**: Vertical inscribed face faces (likely) east or south (away from the heavy lichen growth on top); the **top horizontal surface** receives full vertical sun exposure plus retains dew — the perfect Caloplaca microclimate

### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1 — the orange Caloplaca cap
- **Color**: Vivid yellow-orange to ochre
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, **placodioid** (raised lobed margins around a central cracked area)
- **Growth pattern**: Discrete rosettes ~10–25 mm in diameter coalescing into a near-continuous mat across the top surface; numerous small black apothecia visible in the macro shots
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Dense apothecia (darker centres within the orange thallus), characteristic of fertile Caloplaca
- **Substrate interaction**: Tightly bonded to the substrate; no lifting; clear margin where the colony meets bare stone
- **Approx. coverage**: **Dominant** on the horizontal top surface — ~50–70 % cover; on the front (inscribed) face essentially absent
- **Likely genus / species**: ***Caloplaca aurantia*** (Teloschistaceae) — `medium-high` confidence
- **Reasoning**: Bright orange placodioid rosettes with marginal lobes and apothecial centres on Jerusalem limestone is the textbook signature of *C. aurantia*; one of the species explicitly listed in **Galun & Haluwani (1977)** for Jerusalem tombstones.

#### Lichen #2 — the grey-white background crust
- **Color**: Grey-white, blending into bare stone
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, smooth to weakly rimose-areolate
- **Growth pattern**: Background film occupying the gaps between the orange rosettes
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Not clearly resolved at this resolution
- **Approx. coverage**: ~15–25 % of the horizontal top surface
- **Likely genus**: ***Aspicilia*** (likely *A. calcarea*) — `medium` confidence
- **Reasoning**: Grey-white background crust on calcareous substrate, flush with stone, is classic *Aspicilia*. Could also include *Lecanora muralis* — disambiguation requires apothecial detail not resolvable here.

#### Lichen #3 — the dark perithecial stippling
- **Color**: Black dots, mostly within the orange colony and along its margin
- **Thallus type**: Endolithic-suspected; the visible black points are likely perithecial ostioles
- **Growth pattern**: Scattered, sometimes within the Caloplaca thallus
- **Approx. coverage**: ~5–10 % point coverage
- **Likely genus**: ***Verrucaria*** (likely *V. nigrescens* on calcareous stone) — `medium` confidence
- **Reasoning**: Black flask-shaped fruiting bodies sunken into a calcareous substrate is the classic Verrucaria signature. The *endolithic* thallus inside the stone is exactly the «2 mm זוֹן» the project wants to interrogate — these dark stippled patches on the front face (faintly visible in IMG_3974/_3975) are the surface tip of an extensive subsurface colony.

### Ecology & interpretation
- **Within-stone aspect contrast**: The same stone hosts ~50–70 % cover on its horizontal top and ~<5 % cover on its vertical inscribed face. This is a **textbook in-situ demonstration of the project's «גאפ תרמי»** (thermal-gap) and **«גאפ לחות»** (moisture-gap) hypotheses: the horizontal top retains dew and receives all-day sun, while the front face sheds water and faces (likely) east or south but at a much steeper angle.
- **Why is this stone such a good Caloplaca habitat on top?** White marble reflects UV but does not impede water retention in the porous calcareous matrix; the horizontal cap forms a small water-collecting basin where dew and rain pool briefly each morning before evaporating — exactly the duty cycle Mediterranean Caloplaca thrives on.
- **The contrast with the inscribed face** would be one of the most photogenic «before / after» pairings for the project's exhibition triptych — a single stone simultaneously cleaned and inhabited, depending only on which surface you photograph.
- **Thematic note**: the epitaph (1 Cor. 15:43 — "sown in weakness, raised in power") uses an agricultural sowing metaphor parallel to GS01's epitaph (Psalm 126:5 — "those who sow in tears shall reap in joy"). Both stones use the sowing/resurrection metaphor — and on this stone the metaphor is materially literal: a fertile horizontal "field" of Caloplaca apothecia *literally sown* on stone meant for permanence.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The genus-level IDs above (*Caloplaca, Aspicilia, Verrucaria*) are high-confidence morphological matches; the species-level guesses (*C. aurantia, A. calcarea, V. nigrescens*) follow Galun & Haluwani (1977) for Jerusalem tombstones but should be confirmed by spot tests.

### Photos analyzed
- IMG_3957.jpeg — brick-red crustose patch with moss in carved crevice; caliper visible
- IMG_3958.jpeg — same brick-red patch, different angle; caliper measurement
- IMG_3959.jpeg — caliper measurement of brick-red patch (digital readout ~27 mm)
- IMG_3960.jpeg — wider context of same brick-red zone with yellow-green lichen
- IMG_3961.jpeg — close-up of carved text "Off. 14." on upper obelisk stone face
- IMG_3962.jpeg — dense yellow-green granular thallus with orange apothecia (lecanorine type)
- IMG_3963.jpeg — stone plinth/base; bright yellow-orange lobate thalli on moulding

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: Marble (pinkish-cream, smooth-polished plaque surface; grey-white marble obelisk column) — warmer, more varied tonality than standard Jerusalem limestone
- **Surface condition**: Moderately weathered; plaque face relatively smooth; architectural mouldings and carved ornamental ledges on column; carved recesses accumulate moisture and organic debris
- **Aspect (if inferable from photo)**: Vertical face; stone orientation and lichen distribution suggest south-facing or exposed aspect (bright lichen coverage)

### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1
- **Color**: Brick-red to terracotta-orange
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, granular-areolate (no lobes visible)
- **Growth pattern**: Irregular discrete patches, ~25–30 mm diameter (confirmed by caliper in IMG_3959); found in carved recesses and crevices
- **Reproductive structures visible**: None clearly resolvable
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with or slightly recessed into stone surface; found preferentially in carved/recessed zones
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate (~10–15% of close-up fields; localised)
- **Likely genus**: **_Caloplaca_** sp. (atypical morphotype / possible _C. variabilis_ or iron-contaminated substrate)
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Brick-red colour is unusual for typical orange _Caloplaca aurantia_; the more reddish hue may indicate a different _Caloplaca_ species (e.g., _C. variabilis_, _C. flavovirescens_), an older/senescing thallus, or iron leaching from stone metal hardware altering thallus pigmentation. Spatial association with carved recesses and crevices is consistent with moisture-dependent lichen establishment. Caliper measurement confirms patch diameter ~27 mm.

#### Lichen #2
- **Color**: Yellow-green to bright green
- **Thallus type**: Granular crustose
- **Growth pattern**: Dense granular mat surrounding brick-red patches; also present as scattered dots on stone surface
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Small apothecia visible (orange, ~0.3–0.5 mm)
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate (~20–25% of close-up fields)
- **Likely genus**: **_Candelariella_** sp.
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Yellow-green granular thallus with orange apothecia on calcareous/marble substrate matches _Candelariella_ spp.; the vivid yellow-green colour and granular (not lobate) texture is consistent with _C. vitellina_ or _C. aurella_.

#### Lichen #3
- **Color**: Bright yellow-orange (distinct from brick-red Lichen #1)
- **Thallus type**: Placodioid (lobate)
- **Growth pattern**: Rosette; visible on stone plinth/base mouldings (IMG_3963)
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Not clearly resolved on base shots
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with rounded stone moulding surface
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate (~20–30% of plinth surface visible in IMG_3963)
- **Likely genus**: **_Caloplaca_** (likely _C. aurantia_)
- **Confidence in ID**: `high`
- **Reasoning**: Bright yellow-orange placodioid rosettes on stone base moulding — classic _Caloplaca aurantia_ morphology, identical to that observed in GS01 cluster and consistent with the expected Jerusalem core community.

#### Lichen #4 (non-lichen)
- **Color**: Green
- **Thallus type**: Leafy/bryophytic (not a lichen)
- **Growth pattern**: Tufts growing in carved crevices alongside brick-red lichen patches
- **Approx. coverage**: Trace (~5% of crevice surfaces)
- **Likely taxon**: **Moss (Bryophyta)** — unidentified genus
- **Confidence in ID**: `high`
- **Reasoning**: Leafy photosynthetic structures with visible leaf-like differentiation visible in IMG_3957–IMG_3960; clearly distinct from crustose lichen morphology.

### Ecology & interpretation
- The marble substrate of GS03 differs from the basalt/dark-stone of GS01 and may support a distinct lichen community. Marble is less porous than limestone but still calcareous.
- Brick-red crustose patches specifically in carved recesses suggest moisture-dependent lichen establishment (recesses retain rainwater and resist desiccation).
- Caliper measurement (~27 mm) in the field confirms intentional documentation of this unusual morphotype for size/growth-rate context.
- Moss co-occurring with brick-red lichen in recesses indicates persistent moisture — biologically important for the research question on moisture microclimate effects on lichen colonization (one of the four project research gaps).
- Bright yellow-orange _Caloplaca_ rosettes on the base plinth mouldings (convex horizontal surfaces) parallel observations in GS01 and GS05 — consistent with _Caloplaca aurantia_ preference for convex exposed surfaces.
- Notable: this stone bears two separate biblical epitaphs (Hebrews 13:14 on main plaque; Revelation 14:13 on upper section). The Rev. 14:13 text also appears on GS04 (Eppinger). This verse ("Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord") appears to have been a popular Tempelgesellschaft funerary text.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). Where the photo is ambiguous, this is noted explicitly. The brick-red morphotype (Lichen #1) is specifically flagged as requiring closer examination — field spot-testing and microscopy are recommended.

- This dark, low-diversity community may indicate: (a) a more shaded or sheltered microposition within the cemetery (less direct sunlight slows _Caloplaca_ and _Lecanora_ colonisation); (b) moisture retention by a horizontal flat surface in a lower-drainage position; (c) the extreme weathering of the stone itself, which may have disrupted earlier lichen communities by removing the surface layer.
- Alternatively, the absence of orange/yellow _Caloplaca_ could reflect a genuinely different succession stage or local substrate chemistry.
- Stone age cannot be reliably calculated (death date illegible); if born 1805 [?] and the person died in, e.g., 1875–1890, the stone would be 135–150+ years old at survey — the oldest possible in this batch. Extended age with heavy weathering would support the observed high biological coverage and surface degradation.
- The carved floral/botanical relief is itself a substrate for lichen, with engraved relief channels potentially retaining moisture and accelerating colonisation in the decorated zone.
- A follow-up visit using raking light photography (or RTI) would both assist inscription recovery and provide better lichen documentation.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). For this stone, lichen identification is additionally limited by the poor surface condition of the stone and the near-total absence of visible reproductive structures. The dark community (Lichen #1) is assigned to _Verrucaria_ as the most probable genus given the substrate and colour, but this is a provisional assignment only.

## 🦠 Lichen Analysis

### Photos analyzed
- IMG_4067.jpeg — grey pillar surface, grey-white crustose patches
- IMG_4068.jpeg — dense orange + green lichen mix on stone face
- IMG_4070.jpeg — remarkable placodioid rosette (green-grey thallus + orange-amber apothecia)
- IMG_4071.jpeg — same rosette, slightly different angle
- IMG_4072.jpeg — letter grooves colonized by grey-green crustose lichen
- IMG_4073.jpeg — extreme close-up of engraved letter, granular crustose + yellow specks

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: Jerusalem limestone (calcareous) — white/cream, medium-grained; typical local nari limestone
- **Surface condition**: Weathered; rough on exposed faces; partially smooth where originally dressed. Engraved letters still legible but showing edge dissolution.
- **Aspect (if inferable)**: Mixed — multiple faces of monument; orange Caloplaca suggests direct sun exposure on at least one face (south or west).

### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1 — Grey-white crustose, pillar surface
- **Color**: Grey-white to pale grey
- **Thallus type**: Crustose
- **Growth pattern**: Continuous mat with areolate cracking; spreading patches ~5–15 cm diameter
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Apothecia not clearly resolved — dark specks may be lecideine or lecanorine apothecia
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone surface; etching of carbonate substrate visible at thallus margins
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate to dominant on pillar faces (~40–60%)
- **Likely genus**: ***Aspicilia*** sp. (possibly *A. calcarea*)
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Grey-white areolate crustose thallus on limestone is consistent with *Aspicilia calcarea*, the most common calcareous-substrate crustose in Mediterranean Jerusalem; absence of distinct ring structure rules out *Lecanora* sensu stricto at this scale.

#### Lichen #2 — Orange crustose, close proximity to green
- **Color**: Orange to orange-red
- **Thallus type**: Crustose to placodioid
- **Growth pattern**: Irregular patches, intermingled with green crustose at contact zones
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Orange apothecia visible; lecanorine type suspected
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone, some marginal lifting
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate (~20–30% of this face)
- **Likely genus**: ***Caloplaca*** sp. (possibly *C. aurantia* or *C. variabilis*)
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Orange placodioid/crustose on calcareous substrate in Jerusalem is characteristic of the *Caloplaca* (Teloschistaceae) complex; *C. aurantia* is the expected dominant orange species on limestone in this community.

#### Lichen #3 — Green-grey placodioid rosette with dense orange-amber apothecia ⭐ Notable specimen
- **Color**: Thallus grey-green; apothecia orange-amber to rust-orange
- **Thallus type**: Placodioid — clearly lobate margins, rosette form
- **Growth pattern**: Single large rosette, lobes radiating from center; center densely packed with apothecia
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Apothecia very densely packed, lecanorine type, orange-amber; disc slightly concave to flat
- **Substrate interaction**: Spreading over stone surface; lobes adnate to slightly raised
- **Approx. coverage**: Single rosette ~3–5 cm diameter; locally dominant
- **Likely genus**: ***Caloplaca*** sp. with strongly expressed grey-green thallus; alternatively ***Squamarina*** sp.
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: The grey-green thallus color is atypical for *Caloplaca aurantia* (usually yellow-orange throughout) but the dense orange apothecia strongly suggest Teloschistaceae. *Squamarina* has squamulose (scale-like) lobes rather than placodioid; *Caloplaca saxicola* s.l. can show grey-green thallus with orange apothecia. Microscopy and K+ (Caloplaca = K+ red) spot test needed for confirmation.

#### Lichen #4 — Grey-green crustose in engraved letter grooves
- **Color**: Grey-green
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, granular
- **Growth pattern**: Colonizing engraved letter channels; spreading from groove floors onto surrounding stone
- **Reproductive structures visible**: None clearly visible at this scale
- **Substrate interaction**: Fills grooves; apparent endolithic extension suspected
- **Approx. coverage**: Locally dominant inside grooves; trace on flat surfaces
- **Likely genus**: ***Lecanora*** sp. or ***Aspicilia*** sp.
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Grey-green granular crustose inside limestone letter channels; *Lecanora* and *Aspicilia* are both expected in this niche. The groove microenvironment (shade, moisture retention) differs from open face — could support a different species than the dominant face lichen.

#### Lichen #5 — Yellow specks in letter grooves
- **Color**: Bright yellow
- **Thallus type**: Crustose, granular/powdery
- **Growth pattern**: Scattered specks among grey-green crust
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Granular — may be soredia or granular thallus
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with groove surface
- **Approx. coverage**: Trace (<5%)
- **Likely genus**: ***Candelariella*** sp.
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Bright yellow granular/powdery crustose in grooves is consistent with *Candelariella* (Candelariellaceae), which is frequently found in sheltered niche habitats on calcareous substrates; alternative is *Caloplaca* s.l. in immature or sterile state.

### Ecology & interpretation
- **Aspect**: The distribution of orange *Caloplaca* (requiring direct UV exposure) on the upper/outer stone faces suggests at least one sun-exposed face, likely south or west-facing. The grey crustose dominates on less-exposed faces.
- **Community age signal**: The dense *Aspicilia* coverage (40–60%) on a memorial erected post-1948 (after the expulsions) implies several decades of colonization; crustose coverage of this density on Jerusalem limestone is consistent with 30–60+ years undisturbed growth (Galun & Haluwani 1977 lichen growth rates).
- **Letter-groove colonization** (Lichens #4 and #5): A key bio-design observation for this project — groove colonization follows a different successional pathway than open faces. Grooves retain moisture longer, are shielded from direct UV, and accumulate wind-blown organic material, creating a microhabitat that supports different species assemblages. Over time, groove colonization progressively obscures inscription legibility — the "lichen as memory eraser" dynamic is visible in action here.
- **Pollution tolerance**: Presence of *Caloplaca* and *Aspicilia* but apparent absence of foliose species (e.g., *Physcia*, *Xanthoria*) is consistent with the moderate urban pollution baseline of the German Colony / Emek Refaim neighbourhood.
- **Notable specimen**: Lichen #3 (green-grey placodioid rosette with dense orange apothecia) is the most visually and scientifically interesting organism in this cluster. Its unusual grey-green thallus color warrants targeted species-level investigation.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). Where the photo is ambiguous, this is noted explicitly. Lichen #3 in particular requires physical examination.

- IMG_4085.jpeg — stone surface showing green algal/cyanobacterial film and bright yellow-orange Caloplaca placodioid rosettes on rough limestone

- **Material**: Jerusalem limestone (calcareous) — rough surface texture, cream to light grey; medium to coarse grained
- **Surface condition**: Rough, weathered; significant surface spalling/exfoliation; heavily colonized. The stone surface is in an advanced state of biological coverage.
- **Aspect (if inferable)**: Mixed — both shaded base (moss) and more exposed face (Caloplaca dominant) visible. Caloplaca concentration suggests at least partial sun exposure (south or west face likely).

### Lichen community observed

#### Lichen #1 — Yellow-orange Caloplaca placodioid rosettes ⭐ Dominant species
- **Color**: Bright yellow-orange to orange
- **Thallus type**: Placodioid — clearly lobate, rosette-forming
- **Growth pattern**: Multiple discrete rosettes, 1–5 cm diameter, some beginning to coalesce; radiating lobes clearly visible in close-up
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Apothecia visible — darker orange-red discs in rosette centres; lecanorine type
- **Substrate interaction**: Adnate to rough limestone; lobes spreading across surface spalling and crack edges; actively colonizing rough texture
- **Approx. coverage**: Dominant on exposed faces (~30–50%)
- **Likely genus**: ***Caloplaca*** sp. (likely *C. aurantia* — the diagnostic orange placodioid Jerusalem limestone species)
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium-high`
- **Reasoning**: Bright orange placodioid rosettes with lobate margins and orange lecanorine apothecia on rough calcareous substrate in Mediterranean Jerusalem is the textbook description of *Caloplaca aurantia*. The yellow-orange coloration (vs. deeper orange-red of some species) and the clearly placodioid thallus on limestone are diagnostic. K+ red reaction (xanthones) would confirm Teloschistaceae — not tested.

#### Lichen #2 — Grey-white areolate crustose (Aspicilia)
- **Color**: Grey-white to pale grey
- **Thallus type**: Crustose — areolate (cracked into irregular polygonal islands)
- **Growth pattern**: Continuous background mat between and around Caloplaca rosettes; covering roughened stone surfaces
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Not clearly resolved
- **Substrate interaction**: Flush with stone surface; appears to predate Caloplaca colonization in some areas (Caloplaca growing over Aspicilia background)
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate to dominant as background matrix (~30–40%)
- **Likely genus**: ***Aspicilia*** sp. (possibly *A. calcarea*)
- **Confidence in ID**: `medium`
- **Reasoning**: Grey-white areolate crustose on rough limestone, forming the background community to Caloplaca, is characteristic of *Aspicilia calcarea* in the Jerusalem limestone community. The areolate pattern is distinct from smoother *Lecanora* morphology.

#### Lichen #3 — Green algal/cyanobacterial film
- **Color**: Green
- **Thallus type**: Algal biofilm / proto-crustose
- **Growth pattern**: Diffuse film on stone surfaces, particularly where moisture is retained (hollows, near moss); not a distinct thallus
- **Reproductive structures visible**: None
- **Substrate interaction**: Surface coating and possible endolithic penetration
- **Approx. coverage**: Trace to moderate (~10–15%), concentrated in shaded/moist zones
- **Likely genus**: Cyanobacteria or chlorophyte algae — *Trentepohlia* sp. (orange-green, on rough surfaces) or *Prasiola* sp.; alternatively early stage of Aspicilia/Lecanora photobiont without established mycobiont
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: Green film on limestone in moist zones is typical of photosynthetic microorganisms that precede or accompany lichen establishment; species-level resolution requires microscopy.

#### Lichen #4 — Moss mat at stone base (note from IMG_4084)
- **Color**: Green (slightly darker/yellower than GS26 moss — possibly less moisture)
- **Thallus type**: Bryophyte (not a lichen)
- **Growth pattern**: Mat at stone base; thinner than GS26
- **Reproductive structures visible**: Not resolved
- **Substrate interaction**: Stone-soil interface; thinner coverage than GS26 suggests less shade/moisture here
- **Approx. coverage**: Moderate at stone base (~20–30%)
- **Likely genus**: ***Bryum*** sp. or ***Tortula*** sp. (as for GS24)
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`

### Ecology & interpretation
- **Caloplaca-dominated community**: This stone represents a mature lichen colonization state for exposed Jerusalem limestone — *Caloplaca* as the conspicuous dominant, with *Aspicilia* forming the background matrix. This two-species dominated community is exactly the expected "mature equilibrium" state for calcareous Mediterranean cemetery stones in moderate sun exposure (Galun & Haluwani 1977).
- **Community age signal**: The density of *Caloplaca* rosettes (some beginning to coalesce) and the *Aspicilia* background coverage suggest a stone that has been undisturbed for several decades — consistent with the Templer cemetery period (1870s–1940s for original stones, plus post-establishment years of undisturbed growth after cemetery fell out of active maintenance use).
- **Caliper measurement (~78 mm, IMG_4084)**: This is a key quantitative data point. If this measures a lichen patch diameter, it documents an unusually large *Caloplaca* rosette (78 mm = 7.8 cm diameter), which at growth rates of ~1–3 mm/year for *Caloplaca* on Jerusalem limestone would imply 25–78 years of growth — consistent with mid-20th century stone age. If it measures stone thickness, it documents a relatively thick stone edge. Clarification of what the caliper is measuring in this image is recommended.
- **Surface spalling and lichen succession**: The rough, spalling limestone surface provides an increased surface area for colonization and multiple microhabitats (crack edges, spall surfaces, protected hollows) — driving the diversity and density of colonization observed here.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). The IDs above are best-effort visual matches against the expected Jerusalem-limestone Mediterranean community (Galun & Haluwani 1977; Galun & Mukhtar 1996). *Caloplaca aurantia* is the most confident ID in this cluster; the green film genus remains unresolved.

## 🦠 Lichen Analysis

### Photos analyzed
- IMG_4087.jpeg — full stone view / context: stone with green moss mat and visible red flower stamen
- IMG_4088.jpeg — extreme macro close-up of moss mat surface: individual "leaves" (phyllids) visible, wet/glistening surface

### Stone substrate
- **Material**: Inferred limestone (calcareous) — the stone substrate is almost entirely obscured by moss and is not visible in either photo. Substrate identification is based on the expected material for this cemetery.
- **Surface condition**: Not visible — entirely covered. The presence of a thick, healthy moss mat implies a consistently moist stone surface.
- **Aspect (if inferable)**: The abundance and health of the moss strongly implies a **north-facing** or **deeply shaded** aspect. In Jerusalem's climate (annual precipitation ~550 mm, concentrated in winter; long hot dry summers), a dense, actively growing summer/spring moss mat is only possible on a stone that maintains high surface moisture through shade. This is almost certainly one of the most shaded positions in this area of the cemetery — near a wall, under dense tree cover, or in a low-lying moisture-accumulating position.

### Lichen community observed

*Note: This stone is anomalous — bryophyte (moss) completely dominates. True lichen coverage is minimal or unobservable beneath the moss mat. This cluster documents the extreme "moisture gap" end of the substrate colonization gradient in the GS22–26 series.*

#### Lichen #1 — Green bryophyte (moss) mat ⭐ DOMINANT — ~90%+ coverage
- **Color**: Green, vivid and uniform — indicating active, healthy growth with adequate moisture and light
- **Thallus type**: Bryophyte (moss) — NOT a lichen; documented here as the dominant colonizer
- **Growth pattern**: Continuous, dense mat covering virtually the entire visible stone face and extending down to soil level; individual phyllids (leaf-like structures) clearly visible at macro scale (IMG_4088)
- **Reproductive structures visible**: No sporophytes resolved in close-up; phyllid structure confirms moss (not liverwort)
- **Substrate interaction**: Growing against stone face, retaining moisture against the stone surface; likely accelerating calcium carbonate dissolution through organic acid production and moisture retention
- **Approx. coverage**: Dominant — ~90–95% of visible stone face
- **Likely genus**: ***Bryum*** sp. or ***Homalothecium*** sp. or ***Brachythecium*** sp.
- **Confidence in ID**: `low`
- **Reasoning**: The phyllid morphology visible in IMG_4088 shows upright, densely packed leaves consistent with acrocarpous mosses (e.g., *Bryum*), rather than the flattened, pinnate branching of pleurocarpous mosses (e.g., *Brachythecium*). *Bryum argenteum* is extremely common on calcareous urban surfaces in the Mediterranean; however, genus-level resolution from a single macro photo is unreliable. Bryologist examination recommended.

#### Lichen #2 — Any lichen beneath/between moss (inferred, not visible)
- **Notes**: Any underlying lichen community is completely masked by the moss mat. Based on adjacent GS24 and GS25 stones, it is likely that *Aspicilia* crustose and possibly early *Caloplaca* colonization exists on the stone surface beneath the moss. This cannot be confirmed without physical examination.

### Ecology & interpretation
- **Ecological anomaly in the GS22–26 series**: GS26 is the outlier. While GS22, GS24, and GS25 all show the expected Jerusalem calcareous lichen community (*Caloplaca* + *Aspicilia* ± moss at base), GS26 is bryophyte-dominated across the entire face. This represents either:
  1. **Extreme shade position**: A north-facing stone under tree/wall shade that maintains surface moisture even through Jerusalem's summer — preventing the UV exposure that *Caloplaca* requires and maintaining the humidity that moss needs.
  2. **Low-lying moisture accumulation**: A stone at a topographic low point where water drains toward it, or near a water source (irrigation pipe, drainage channel).
  3. **Fallen stone or near-horizontal surface**: If this stone has fallen or tilted, a near-horizontal surface would accumulate rain water and soil particles differently from a vertical face, dramatically accelerating moss growth.
- **Moisture gap (project framework)**: GS26 exemplifies the "moisture gap" in the project's 4-gap bio-design framework. Where moisture is abundant and sustained (this stone), the community shifts from lichen-dominated to bryophyte-dominated — a fundamentally different successional trajectory.
- **Memory obliteration**: GS26 represents the most advanced state of "inscription obliteration by biological colonization" in this cluster series. If the inscription cannot be read from the opposite stone face, this individual's identity has been effectively erased by the moss mat — a poignant intersection of biology and cultural memory relevant to the project's research framing.
- **Red flower stamen**: The fallen stamen (visible in IMG_4087) is not a biological colonizer but is notable as evidence of the cultural/memorial layer still present in this cemetery — someone brought flowers, or a flowering plant grows immediately adjacent.
- **Conservation concern**: A moss mat of this density and coverage actively traps moisture against the stone and produces organic acids during decomposition. This is one of the most active stone dissolution scenarios in the GS22–26 series and may warrant documentation for conservation purposes.

### Uncertainty notes
> [!warning] Limits of photo-only identification
> Photo-based lichen ID is reliable to genus level for distinctive species but cannot confirm species without microscopy and chemical spot tests (K, C, KC, P, UV reactions). For this cluster, the bryophyte identification is the primary challenge — moss genus/species determination requires microscopy of phyllid cell structure, costa morphology, and sporophyte anatomy. The lichen community beneath the moss cannot be assessed from these photos. Physical examination required for any species-level determination.
